meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users at baseline exhibited substantially higher obesity rates (BMI 30.0–39.9 kg/m²: 13.21% vs 4.87% in metformin and 3.04% in insulin) and higher socioeconomic status (undergraduate and above: 26.07% vs 11.94% in metformin) in Table 3S. Propensity score matching handled missing BMI (32.49% to 33.81%) and education by matching 'unspecified' categories directly rather than imputing or measuring true values, leaving substantial residual confounding and confounding by indication that inflates hazard ratios away from the null (e.g., renal failure sHR 3.73, leukemia sHR 15.09).

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Out of 985,278 initial diabetes outpatients, 177,381 were excluded for missing IDs and 362,035 were excluded for missing prescription data (over 54% excluded on missing data alone), creating a highly selected survivor/active-user cohort prone to selection bias that exaggerates rate differences away from the null.

findings.title: Massive attrition from missing record linkage and prescription data
findings.mechanism: Excluding over half the target clinical population based on data completeness in administrative databases can induce selection bias if data completeness correlates with health-seeking behavior, healthcare utilization, and adverse event recording.

362,035 outpatients excluded due to missing prescription data (Figure 1)
Only 380,370 of 985,278 outpatients remained eligible at baseline (Figure 1)

domains.direction_justification: Concomitant medications, treatment switching, and subsequent clinical interventions during the mean follow-up of 23.2–24.8 months were not dynamically adjusted in the time-to-event models.

findings.title: Uncontrolled post-baseline therapeutic modifications
findings.mechanism: Patients initiating new add-on medications or discontinuing therapy during follow-up beyond the initial inclusion criteria could alter downstream organ risk independently of the baseline exposure.
evidence: Mean follow-up was 23.7 ± 18.5 months for GLP-1 RAs, 23.2 ± 18.3 months for insulin, and 24.8 ± 18.6 months for metformin

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Key matching variables contained high levels of missingness (HbA1c >90%, FPG ~30%, BMI ~33%), and 'unspecified' status was matched directly between arms (e.g., 32.49% unspecified BMI in GLP-1 RA matched to 32.71% in metformin), preventing true balance of these critical risk factors.

findings.title: Matching on missingness categories rather than complete/imputed clinical variables
findings.mechanism: Treating missing data as an explicit matching category ('Unspecified') ensures demographic balance in missingness proportions but leaves actual biological imbalance unaddressed.

Education unspecified was 33.62% vs 35.89% (Table 1)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users represent higher socioeconomic status (26.07% undergraduate vs 11.94% in metformin) with higher citizen health insurance coverage (75.60% vs 54.96% in metformin) and are subject to closer clinical monitoring/diagnostic workups due to known drug warnings (e.g., thyroid ultrasound, renal panels), creating surveillance/detection bias that systematically increases event ascertainment away from the null.

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias
findings.mechanism: Outcomes such as thyroid cancer, thyroid dysfunction, and acute nephritis were ascertained via electronic diagnosis codes and free-text regex without blinded adjudication. Higher monitoring frequency in patients on novel injectable therapies inflates diagnosis rates.
evidence: Outcomes identified via ICD-10 and regular expression string matching across outpatient and hospitalization records (Table 2S)
Higher baseline health insurance (75.60% vs 54.96%) and education (26.07% vs 11.94%) in GLP-1 RA vs metformin group (Table 3S)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Multiple hypothesis testing across 20+ disease outcomes, multiple sub-agents, and duration strata without pre-registered analysis protocols or multiplicity corrections leads to selective prominence of extreme effect sizes (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65–48.98; acne sHR 5.32, 95% CI 2.21–12.81).

findings.title: Multiple testing and outcome multiplicity without pre-specified protocol
findings.mechanism: Testing numerous exploratory outcome categories across multiple comparator arms and subgroup durations increases the likelihood of reporting statistically significant, extreme hazard ratios driven by small event counts.
evidence: Over 20 distinct adverse outcomes tested across 6 body systems (Table 2S)
Extreme effect estimates reported for rare outcomes (leukemia sHR: 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65–48.98; acne sHR: 5.32, 95% CI: 2.21–12.81 in Figure 3)

overall.summary: This retrospective observational cohort study evaluated adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use compared to insulin and metformin monotherapies in Shenzhen, China. The study is at very high overall risk of bias due to critical unmeasured and residual confounding (over 90% missing baseline HbA1c, ~33% missing BMI matched as 'unspecified' categories), severe selection attrition (>50% excluded due to missing IDs/prescriptions), surveillance bias (increased diagnostic monitoring in newer injectable therapy users), and multiplicity of outcomes without pre-specified analysis plans, leading to biologically implausible associations (e.g., sHR 15.09 for leukemia) heavily biased away from the null.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event counts and incidence rates per outcome category in matched and unmatched cohorts (only sHRs and CIs are provided in the text/figures).
Baseline diabetes duration, baseline eGFR/renal function, and smoking/alcohol history to evaluate baseline comparability across treatment groups.
Data on complete HbA1c and BMI values for the ~91% and ~33% missing records to assess the extent of residual confounding.

baseline_comparability.summary: The GLP-1 RA cohort had markedly higher baseline obesity and substantially higher healthcare coverage and education compared to the insulin and metformin control groups. Matching on 'unspecified' categories failed to address massive missingness (>90% missing HbA1c, >32% missing BMI), leaving substantial detection and indication biases driving the observed adverse risk estimates away from the null.

timeline.study_period: from the date of the first medical record included on January 1, 2016 to the last database update on September 1, 2022
timeline.follow_up: The mean follow-up time was 23.7 ± 18.5, 23.2 ± 18.3, and 24.8 ± 18.6 months for the GLP-1 RAs, insulin-only, and metformin-only groups, respectively
timeline.exposure_definition: The GLP-1 RAs group was defined as any T2D patients who mainly prescribed GLP-1 RAs lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up while the accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months
timeline.cohort_entry_rule: All incidence duration/survival times for outcomes of interest were operationalized as the number of months from the initial outpatient date at baseline to the occurrence of the first recorded hospitalization/outpatient events, whichever came first

design.why: The GLP-1 RAs group was defined as any T2D patients who mainly prescribed GLP-1 RAs lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up while the accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months. Additionally, this study integrated two control groups of T2D patients, namely those mainly receiving insulin therapy and those mainly receiving metformin therapy... lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up date
design.selects_for: Selects survivors and adherent patients who maintained predominant medication patterns through the entire follow-up period without switching treatments

immortal_time.which_group: GLP-1 RAs, insulin-only, and metformin-only groups
immortal_time.duration: Variable interval across follow-up required to accrue predominant prescription status
immortal_time.why: Treatment group assignment depends on prescriptions received throughout total follow-up ('lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up date'), requiring patients to survive and remain under care long enough to meet exposure group definitions

lag_and_latency.follow_up_vs_latency: Mean follow-up was 23.7 months (~1.98 years; derived: 23.7 / 12). For slow-growing oncologic outcomes such as thyroid cancer (sHR 2.25 within <12 months) and leukemia, biological latency requires multi-year to decade-long induction periods

duration_gradient.interpretation: While estimates for several outcomes are numerically higher in the >=12 month stratum, solid tumor risks (thyroid cancer sHR 2.25) are already significantly elevated in <12 months of use without a lag period, indicating substantial detection bias and reverse causation of pre-existing disease rather than true de novo drug carcinogenesis

findings.title: Immortal time and future-informed exposure classification
findings.mechanism: Classifying exposure based on cumulative prescriptions across total follow-up ('lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up date') conditions group assignment on future events and survival
evidence: The GLP-1 RAs group was defined as any T2D patients who mainly prescribed GLP-1 RAs lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up while the accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months.

findings.title: Absence of lag period for latent outcomes
findings.mechanism: Failing to exclude early follow-up allows pre-existing subclinical diseases (such as thyroid neoplasms) diagnosed shortly after initiating or switching therapy to be falsely attributed to the exposure
evidence: GLP-1 RAs use under 12 months group appeared to be associated with increased incidence risks of... thyroid cancer (sHR: 2.25, 95% CI: 1.23–4.10)

findings.title: Absence of washout period and new-user design
findings.mechanism: Without a washout window prior to baseline entry date, the cohort includes prevalent users, missing early treatment dropouts and depleting susceptible individuals
evidence: All incidence duration/survival times for outcomes of interest were operationalized as the number of months from the initial outpatient date at baseline to the occurrence of the first recorded hospitalization/outpatient events, whichever came first.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure groups based on predominant medication use over the entire follow-up, introducing immortal time bias and post-baseline conditioning. Furthermore, the complete absence of a lag period for long-latency malignancies leads to immediate risk elevations (<12 months) that reflect reverse causation and detection bias rather than true drug-induced adverse events.
